---
title: "Discrete-time stochastic models"
subtitle: "Otto & Day, chapter 14, with PracticalCAS"
engine: julia
---

Markov chains, genetic drift in the Wright–Fisher and Moran models, and
branching processes. With symbolic parameters, transition matrices give
exact stationary distributions and absorption probabilities, recurrences
give fixation probabilities for any population size, and generating
functions give extinction probabilities.

```{julia}
using PracticalCAS
```

## A two-state Markov chain

A site switches from state 1 to 2 with probability `a` and back with
probability `b` each step. The stationary distribution, and the distribution
after `t` steps (approaching it geometrically, at rate `1 - a - b`):

```{julia}
@syms a::(0, 1) b::(0, 1) t::natural
P = [1-a a; b 1-b]
stationary_distribution(P)
```

```{julia}
Pt = matpow(P, t)
Pt[1, 1]
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
πs = stationary_distribution(P)
@assert isequiv(πs[1], b / (a + b))
@assert isequiv(Pt[1, 1], b / (a + b) + a / (a + b) * (1 - a - b)^t)
```

## Genetic drift: loss of heterozygosity

In a Wright–Fisher population of `N` diploids, the expected heterozygosity
declines by the factor `1 - 1/(2N)` each generation:

```{julia}
@syms N::positive H::(0, 1) H₀::(0, 1)
Ht = rsolve(recurrence(H => (1 - 1 / (2N)) * H), t)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert all(isapprox(evalf(Ht, H₀ => 0.5, N => 10, t => k), 0.5 * (1 - 1 / 20)^k) for k in 0:5)

```

## Fixation in a small population

The transition matrix of the haploid Wright–Fisher model with `N = 3`
individuals; the neutral fixation probability from `i` copies is `i/N`:

```{julia}
wf = wright_fisher(3)
```

```{julia}
fix = absorption(wf, [2, 3], [1, 4])
fix.probabilities
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert all(isequiv.(fix.probabilities[:, 2], [1 // 3, 2 // 3]))
@assert all(isequiv.(sum(wf; dims = 2), 1))
```

With selection the fixation probabilities are exact rational functions of the
selection coefficient. For the Moran model with relative fitness `r`:

```{julia}
@syms r::positive
mo = moran(3; r = r)
absorption(mo, [2, 3], [1, 4]).probabilities[:, 2]
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
pr = absorption(mo, [2, 3], [1, 4]).probabilities[:, 2]
@assert isequiv(pr[1], (1 - 1 / r) / (1 - 1 / r^3))
```

## Fixation for any population size

In the Moran model the number of mutants goes up with probability
proportional to `r i (N - i)` and down with `i (N - i)`. Conditioning on the
first step gives a second-order recurrence for the fixation probability
`x(i)`, with `x(0) = 0` and `x(N) = 1`:

```{julia}
@funs x
@syms i::natural Nₘ::natural
rsolve(x(i + 1) - (1 + r) * x(i) + r * x(i - 1) ~ 0, x(i); bc = [x(0) => 0, x(Nₘ) => 1])
```

Written with the ratio of the down to the up probability, `1/r`, this is
the classical result, which `fixation_probability` computes for any
birth–death chain:

```{julia}
@syms j::natural
ρ = fixation_probability(r * j * (Nₘ - j), j * (Nₘ - j), j, 1, Nₘ)
```

```{julia}
fixation_probability(j * (Nₘ - j), j * (Nₘ - j), j, i, Nₘ)     # neutral
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(ρ, (1 - 1 / r) / (1 - 1 / r^Nₘ))
@assert isequiv(subs(ρ, Nₘ => 3), pr[1])
@assert isequiv(fixation_probability(j * (Nₘ - j), j * (Nₘ - j), j, i, Nₘ), i / Nₘ)
@assert isequiv(rsolve(x(i + 1) - (1 + r) * x(i) + r * x(i - 1) ~ 0, x(i); bc = [x(0) => 0, x(Nₘ) => 1]),
                (r^i - 1) / (r^Nₘ - 1))
```

A beneficial mutation (`r = 1 + s`) in a large population fixes with
probability about `s/(1 + s)`, not 1:

```{julia}
@syms σ::positive
limit(subs(ρ, r => 1 + σ), Nₘ, ∞)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(limit(subs(ρ, r => 1 + σ), Nₘ, ∞), σ / (1 + σ))
```

## Branching processes

Each individual leaves 0 or 2 offspring, 2 with probability `p`. The
offspring generating function is `G(s) = 1 - p + p s²`; the mean is `2p`,
and when it exceeds one the lineage escapes extinction with probability
`1 - q`, where `q` is the smallest root of `G(s) = s`:

```{julia}
@syms s p::(0, 1)
G = 1 - p + p * s^2
pgf_moments(G, s)
```

```{julia}
q = assuming(p > 1 // 2) do
    extinction_probability(G, s)
end
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(q, (1 - p) / p)
@assert isequiv(assuming(() -> extinction_probability(G, s), p < 1 // 2), 1)
```

With Poisson offspring (mean `R`) there is no closed form, but with numbers
the extinction probability is found by iterating `q ← G(q)`:

```{julia}
qp = extinction_probability(exp(2 * (s - 1)), s)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert abs(evalf(qp) - exp(2 * (evalf(qp) - 1))) < 1e-12 && evalf(qp) < 1
```

The generating function of the population size after `t` generations is the
`t`-fold composition of `G`, so the probability of extinction by generation
`t` is `G` applied `t` times to 0:

```{julia}
extinct_by(k) = k == 0 ? toterm(0) : simplify(subs(G, s => extinct_by(k - 1)))
[extinct_by(k) for k in 1:3]
```

With `p = 3/4` these increase to the extinction probability `1/3`:

```{julia}
ext = accumulate((q, _) -> 1 / 4 + 3 / 4 * q^2, 1:12; init = 0.0)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(extinct_by(2), 1 - p + p * (1 - p)^2)
@assert issorted(ext) && abs(ext[end] - 1 / 3) < 1e-3
```


## Simulation

Simulated Wright–Fisher populations agree with the exact fixation
probabilities. With `N = 10`, 2 initial copies and selection `s = 0.2`:

```{julia}
exact = absorption(wright_fisher(10; s = 1 // 5), 2:10, [1, 11]).probabilities[2, 2]
runs = [wright_fisher_path(10, 2, 10_000; s = 0.2)[end] for _ in 1:4000]
evalf(exact), count(==(10), runs) / 4000
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
pe = evalf(exact)
@assert abs(count(==(10), runs) / 4000 - pe) < 5 * sqrt(pe * (1 - pe) / 4000)
@assert 0.2 < pe < 0.6
```
